Radar absorbing material (RAM) typically has low thermal conductivity (~0.5 W/m·K) and high specific heat (~1200 J/kg·K).
Aluminum metal has high thermal conductivity (~205 W/m·K) and lower specific heat (~900 J/kg·K).
Under a uniform heat flux of 200 W/m² applied for 10 seconds, RAM surfaces develop central high-temperature zones with uneven temperature distribution.
Metal surfaces reach thermal stability faster (~1.5 seconds) than RAM (~3.5 seconds).
RAM surfaces showed a maximum temperature of 40.19°C and a mean temperature of 33.81°C under test conditions.
Metal surfaces showed a maximum temperature of 34.05°C and a mean temperature of 32.14°C under the same conditions.
The standard deviation of surface temperature was 3.47°C for RAM and 0.88°C for metal, indicating more uniform temperature on metal.
Uneven temperature distribution on RAM increases infrared (IR) detectability by creating high-contrast hotspots.
RAM's thermal inertia causes delayed heat diffusion and surface temperature saturation over time.
Integrating active IR stealth with radar stealth is challenging due to conflicting thermal properties of RAM and metal substrates.
Three integrated stealth design strategies proposed: local active thermal control, multilayer hierarchical structures, and spatial optimization of thermal inertia.
Active thermal control can be implemented via Peltier elements or fluid circulation modules embedded beneath the surface.
Multilayer structures with intermediate high-conductivity layers can mediate heat transfer between RAM and metal.
Spatial variation of RAM thickness/density can optimize thermal response to reduce IR hotspots while maintaining radar stealth.
Simulated IR images show RAM surfaces produce broader brightness histograms with more high-temperature pixels than metal surfaces.
Effective multispectral stealth requires early-stage integrated design considering both IR and radar stealth constraints.
The study used MuSES software for coupled thermal conduction and radiation simulations.
The test specimen was a 300mm x 300mm x 5mm flat plate with uniform heat flux applied on the top surface.
Side surfaces were insulated, bottom surface had convection boundary conditions with 10 W/m²·K heat transfer coefficient and ambient temperature 25°C.
The paper emphasizes the importance of real-time surface temperature synchronization with background for IR stealth.
RAM is commonly applied as an external coating on metal structures, causing thermal mismatch and control challenges.
The study provides a quantitative basis for designing integrated IR-RF stealth platforms in complex sensor environments.
Thermal response differences between RAM and metal are a fundamental physical asymmetry causing technical conflicts in stealth integration.
Future work includes experimental validation and extension to complex operational scenarios.
